mcqs.question: What is the defining trade-off of an active-passive topology?
options: Exactly one region owns reads and writes at a time, avoiding conflicts, but the standby region's capacity sits idle and failover takes real time
Both regions serve live writes simultaneously, so there is no failover delay at all
It eliminates the need for any data replication between regions
It is only usable for read-only workloads with no writes
mcqs.explanation: Active-passive keeps a single writer, so there's nothing to conflict-resolve, but that simplicity costs idle standby capacity and a real promotion delay during failover. Active-passive still needs continuous replication to keep the standby current, and it supports writes fine — just through one region at a time.

mcqs.question: In a read-local, write-global topology, what happens to a user in Europe writing data while the write-owning region is in the US?
options: Their write is served entirely locally in Europe with no cross-region hop
Their write is redirected across the network to the US owning region, paying full cross-region latency, while their reads stay local and fast
Their write is rejected outright since only local writes are supported
Their write triggers a conflict-resolution process against other regions' writes
mcqs.explanation: Read-local, write-global keeps a single write owner, so a distant user's write has to travel to that owner and pay the round-trip cost — only reads stay local and fast. Writes aren't rejected, and since there's only one writer, there's no cross-region conflict to resolve.

mcqs.question: A team needs every region's write capacity actively used and can tolerate eventual consistency between regions. Which topology fits best?
options: Active-passive
Read-local, write-global
Active-active
Follow-the-sun
mcqs.explanation: Active-active is the only shape where every region accepts writes concurrently, which is exactly what's needed when write capacity must be used everywhere and eventual consistency is acceptable. The other three all funnel writes through a single owning region at any given moment.

mcqs.question: A system serves reads from three regions but routes every write for a given record through one designated region. Which label is accurate?
options: Active-active, since three regions are serving traffic
A stateless system, since reads are distributed
Follow-the-sun, since one region currently owns writes
A single-writer topology such as read-local/write-global — active-active specifically requires every region to accept writes, not just reads
mcqs.explanation: Active-active is defined by write acceptance in every region, not read distribution — a single write owner with distributed reads is read-local/write-global regardless of how many regions look "active." It isn't follow-the-sun unless that ownership deliberately rotates on a schedule, and statelessness is an unrelated property.

mcqs.question: Why does geo-partitioning (assigning each user's data to one home region) avoid the write-conflict problem that active-active has?
options: It uses a stronger consistency model than active-active
Because each user's data has exactly one owning region, so two regions never accept concurrent writes to the same data in the first place
It replicates every write to every region synchronously
It disables writes entirely outside business hours
mcqs.explanation: Geo-partitioning sidesteps conflicts structurally: since a given user's data is only ever written by their home region, there's no second writer to conflict with, unlike active-active where the same record can be written from multiple regions. It's not about a stronger consistency model, synchronous replication everywhere, or disabling writes on a schedule.
